title: A blade of grass in Lanka
hook: a captive in a grove puts a blade of grass between herself and a king, and later turns down her own rescue
carry: sita kept her dharma even as a captive
tomorrow: what does Sita say after the war?

segments.voice: Yesterday, married partners walk one dharma, side by side is earth's daughter, and the earth is mother: told to stay behind, she argued that husband and wife share one dharma, and walked into exile beside Rama.
screen: `MARRIED PARTNERS WALK ONE DHARMA, SIDE BY SIDE IS EARTH'S DAUGHTER, AND THE EARTH IS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: A single blade of grass. In Valmiki's fifth book, the Sundara Kanda, that's what Sita sets down between herself and Ravana. She's a captive in his city of Lanka, kept in a grove of ashoka trees, guarded day and night. He comes to her with jewels, promises and threats. She doesn't look at him. She picks up a blade of grass, places it between them, and speaks to the grass. Today: two choices Sita makes in the grove, both in her own words, and the second is a no to the one who has come to find her.
screen: `A SINGLE BLADE OF GRASS.` → `A CAPTIVE IN THE ASHOKA GROVE.` → `TWO CHOICES, IN HER OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: The first choice is the grass. Ravana offers her his kingdom, and his queens as her servants. Sita answers through the blade of grass, in paraphrase: turn your mind back to your own wives. I am not for you, the way the light belongs to the sun. Give me back to Rama, if you want to live. The grass is a wall made of almost nothing. It says: I won't even speak to you face to face. The second choice comes later. Hanuman, Rama's messenger, slips into the grove and shows her Rama's ring, so she knows he's real. Then he offers: climb on my back, and I'll carry you across the sea. Sita says no, and the text keeps her reasons. You might drop me over the water, or be attacked on the way. I won't willingly touch the body of any man but Rama. And this is Rama's to finish: let him come, defeat Ravana, and take me back himself. Then she gives Hanuman a jewel from her hair and a private memory from the forest, so Rama will know the message is truly hers. That's the teaching tradition draws from the grove: dharma isn't only for easy days. Sita holds hers as a captive, with nothing but a blade of grass and Rama in her mind, and she still sets the terms of her own rescue. It's one reason many Hindus read the Sundara Kanda in hard times: it's the book where a captive holds firm, and hope arrives.
screen: `SHE SPEAKS THROUGH A BLADE OF GRASS` · `THE RING, AND THE OFFER OF A RIDE` · `SITA SAYS NO, AND GIVES REASONS` · `DHARMA HELD, EVEN AS A CAPTIVE`

segments.voice: Sita in the grove kept Rama in mind, day after day. Sit, and with each breath out, silently say a name you trust; many Hindus use Ram. If something keeps pressing on you, let that name sit between you and it, quiet as her blade of grass, and notice you can still choose where your attention goes. If you don't pray, choose one word you'd want to stand on.
Sita. In the ashoka grove, she speaks to Ravana through a blade of grass and turns down Hanuman's offer to carry her home. Today's word.
Your line: Sita kept her dharma even as a captive. A blade of grass can be a wall. Rest well.
